## Notation

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| $i = 1, \ldots, N$ | Index for individuals (choice situations) |
| $j = 1, \ldots, J_i$ | Index for inside alternatives available to individual $i$ |
| $C_i$ | Choice set of inside alternatives available in situation $i$ |
| $j_i$ | The alternative chosen by individual $i$ |
| $w_i$ | Weight for individual $i$ |
| $X_{ij}$ | Row vector of covariates for individual $i$ and alternative $j$ ($1 \times K$) |
| $\beta$ | Coefficient vector ($K \times 1$) |
| $\delta_j$ | Alternative-specific constant (ASC) for alternative $j$ |
| $V_{ij}$ | Systematic (deterministic) utility |
| $B_k$ | Global set of inside alternatives belonging to nest $k$; situation $i$ contributes $B_k\cap C_i$ |
| $k(j)$ | The nest containing alternative $j$ |
| $\lambda_k$ | Inclusive value (dissimilarity) coefficient for nest $k$ |
| $I_k$ | Inclusive value for nest $k$ |
| $P(j \mid k)$ | Probability of choosing $j$ conditional on choosing nest $k$ |
| $P_k$ | Marginal probability of choosing nest $k$ |
| $P_{ij}$ | Probability that individual $i$ chooses alternative $j$ |

---

## 1. Model Definition

### 1.1 Utility Specification

The utility that individual $i$ derives from alternative $j$ is:

$$
U_{ij} = V_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}
$$

where the systematic utility is:

$$
V_{ij} = X_{ij}\beta + \delta_j
$$

The error term $\varepsilon_{ij}$ follows a Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distribution that induces within-nest correlation.

### 1.2 Nest Structure

The $J$ inside alternatives are partitioned into $K$ mutually exclusive and exhaustive nests $B_1, \ldots, B_K$. An outside option (alternative 0) with $V_{i0} = 0$ may optionally be included, and it is always assigned its own singleton nest with $\lambda_0 = 1$.

### 1.3 Inclusive Value Coefficients

Each nest $k$ has a dissimilarity parameter $\lambda_k > 0$ that governs within-nest substitution:

- $\lambda_k = 1$ corresponds to independent (MNL-like) alternatives within the nest.
- $0 < \lambda_k < 1$ indicates positive within-nest correlation (the typical case).
- $\lambda_k > 1$ is mathematically evaluable in the implemented probability formula
  but lies outside the standard globally RUM-consistent nested-GEV restriction
  $0<\lambda_k\leq1$. It should not automatically be interpreted as a valid negative
  within-nest correlation parameter.

The optimizer in `run_nestlogit()` currently imposes the lower bound $\lambda_k > 0$
but does not impose $\lambda_k \leq 1$. An estimate above one should therefore be
read as a diagnostic about the nesting tree or maintained assumptions, not as
evidence of especially strong within-nest substitution.

**Singleton nests** (nests with exactly one alternative) have $\lambda_k$ fixed to 1 and are not estimated. Only non-singleton nests contribute $\lambda$ parameters to $\theta$.
The low-level parser requires at least one globally non-singleton nest; a specification in
which every nest is a singleton is rejected rather than estimated as an MNL through this
entry point.

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

### 1.4 Alternative-Specific Constants (ASCs)

The ASC identification follows the same convention as MNL:

- **Without outside option** (`include_outside_option = FALSE`): The first inside alternative's ASC is fixed to zero ($\delta_1 = 0$). The parameter vector contains $J-1$ free ASC parameters.
- **With outside option** (`include_outside_option = TRUE`): The outside option serves as the reference with $V_{i0} = 0$. All $J$ inside alternatives have free ASC parameters.

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

---

## 2. Log-Likelihood Function

### 2.1 Probability Decomposition

The nested logit choice probability decomposes as:

$$
P_{ij} = P(j \mid k(j)) \cdot P_{k(j)}
$$

The two components are derived from the GEV generating function.

### 2.2 Inclusive Value

The inclusive value for nest $k$ is the log-sum of scaled utilities within the nest:

$$
I_{ik} = \sum_{j \in B_k\cap C_i} \exp\!\left(\frac{V_{ij}}{\lambda_k}\right)
$$

$$
\log I_{ik} = \log\!\left(\sum_{j \in B_k\cap C_i} \exp\!\left(\frac{V_{ij}}{\lambda_k}\right)\right)
$$

The rest of the article suppresses the $i$ subscript and writes $I_k$. Nests with no
available alternative in $C_i$ have log inclusive value $-\infty$ and contribute zero to
the upper-level denominator.

### 2.3 Conditional Choice Probability

The probability of choosing alternative $j$ given that nest $k(j)$ is chosen:

$$
P(j \mid k) = \frac{\exp(V_{ij}/\lambda_k)}{I_k}
$$

In log form:

$$
\log P(j \mid k) = \frac{V_{ij}}{\lambda_k} - \log I_k
$$

### 2.4 Nest (Marginal) Probability

The probability of choosing nest $k$:

$$
P_k = \frac{\exp(\lambda_k \log I_k)}{\sum_{l} \exp(\lambda_l \log I_l)}
$$

If an outside option is included, its contribution enters the denominator as $\exp(\lambda_0 \log I_0) = \exp(1 \cdot \log(\exp(0/1))) = \exp(0) = 1$.

In log form:

$$
\log P_k = \lambda_k \log I_k - \log\!\left(\sum_l \exp(\lambda_l \log I_l)\right)
$$

### 2.5 Joint Choice Probability

Taking logs of the joint probability:

$$
\log P_{ij} = \log P(j \mid k(j)) + \log P_{k(j)}
$$

$$
\log P_{ij} = \frac{V_{ij}}{\lambda_{k(j)}} - \log I_{k(j)} + \lambda_{k(j)} \log I_{k(j)} - \log D_i
$$

where $D_i = \sum_l \exp(\lambda_l \log I_l)$ (plus 1 if an outside option is present).

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

### 2.6 Log-Likelihood

The log-likelihood is the weighted sum of log-probabilities of the observed choices:

$$
\ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \log P_{ij_i}
$$

where $\theta = (\beta, \lambda, \delta)$ and $j_i$ is the alternative chosen by individual $i$.

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

### 2.7 Log-Sum-Exp Trick for Numerical Stability

Two log-sum-exp stabilizations are applied.

**Within-nest inclusive value.** To compute $\log I_k$ without overflow, the implementation subtracts the maximum scaled utility in each nest:

$$
\log I_k = V_{\max,k} + \log\!\left(\sum_{j \in B_k} \exp\!\left(\frac{V_{ij}}{\lambda_k} - V_{\max,k}\right)\right)
$$

where $V_{\max,k} = \max_{j \in B_k} V_{ij}/\lambda_k$.

**Across-nest denominator.** The denominator $D_i = \sum_l \exp(\lambda_l \log I_l)$ is similarly stabilized by subtracting $\max_l \lambda_l \log I_l$ before exponentiation.

**Nests an individual does not face.** A nest none of whose alternatives individual $i$
faces has $\log I_k = -\infty$, so $\lambda_k \log I_k = -\infty$ when $\lambda_k > 0$: it
never raises the maximum, and its term $\exp(-\infty) = 0$ adds nothing to $D_i$. Where every
$\lambda_k$ is positive and the nests outnumber an individual's alternatives on average, the
kernels therefore form the inclusive values, the maximum and $D_i$ over the nests the
individual faces, in increasing order and in the same two partial sums (by each nest's index
parity) as the loops over every nest, which changes no bit of the result. With a $\lambda_k$
that is NaN, zero or negative (which no exported function accepts), they loop over every
nest.

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

### 2.8 Relation to Other Nested-Logit Parameterizations

The probabilities in §§2.3–2.4 are the utility-normalized GEV form used by
`choicer` (McFadden 1978; Train 2009, Ch. 4): utility is scaled by $1/\lambda_k$
inside the conditional probability, and the inclusive value is multiplied by
$\lambda_k$ in the nest probability. Some software uses a normalization in which its
reported systematic index enters the within-nest logit unscaled. These conventions can
represent different definitions of utility coefficients and error scales; they are not
generally numerically identical under a common-coefficient restriction, and their
reported $\beta$ and $\lambda$ cannot be compared without deriving the normalization
mapping. It is too strong to label every unscaled convention non-RUM; the precise point
is which utility, inclusive-value, and scale normalization is being estimated
(Koppelman & Wen 1998; Hensher & Greene 2002; Heiss 2002).

## 3. Gradient Computation

### 3.1 Gradient with Respect to $V_{ia}$ (Utility Scores)

To derive the gradients with respect to $\beta$ and $\delta$, we first compute the derivative of the log-probability of the chosen alternative with respect to the systematic utility $V_{ia}$ of each alternative $a$.

Let $k_i$ denote the chosen nest (i.e., $k(j_i)$). The log-probability of the chosen alternative is:

$$
\log P_{ij_i} = \log P(j_i \mid k_i) + \log P_{k_i}
$$

**Derivative of the conditional term.** Since $\log P(j \mid k) = V_{ij}/\lambda_k - \log I_k$ and $\frac{\partial \log I_k}{\partial V_{ia}} = \frac{1}{\lambda_k} \mathbf{1}_{a \in B_k} P(a \mid k)$:

$$
\frac{\partial \log P(j_i \mid k_i)}{\partial V_{ia}} = \frac{1}{\lambda_{k_i}}\left(\mathbf{1}_{a = j_i} - \mathbf{1}_{a \in B_{k_i}} P(a \mid k_i)\right)
$$

**Derivative of the nest term.** Using $\frac{\partial \log D_i}{\partial V_{ia}} = P_{k(a)} P(a \mid k(a)) = P_{ia}$:

$$
\frac{\partial \log P_{k_i}}{\partial V_{ia}} = \mathbf{1}_{a \in B_{k_i}} P(a \mid k_i) - P_{ia}
$$

**Combined.** Adding both terms:

$$
\frac{\partial \log P_{ij_i}}{\partial V_{ia}} = \frac{\mathbf{1}_{a = j_i}}{\lambda_{k_i}} + \left(1 - \frac{1}{\lambda_{k_i}}\right)\mathbf{1}_{a \in B_{k_i}} P(a \mid k_i) - P_{ia}
$$

This is implemented as the vector `grad_vec` of length $J_i$:

$$
\text{grad\_vec}[a] = -P_{ia} + \left(1 - \frac{1}{\lambda_{k_i}}\right) \mathbf{1}_{a \in B_{k_i}} P(a \mid k_i) + \frac{1}{\lambda_{k_i}} \mathbf{1}_{a = j_i}
$$

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

### 3.2 Gradient with Respect to $\beta$

Since $\frac{\partial V_{ij}}{\partial \beta} = X_{ij}^T$, the contribution from individual $i$ is:

$$
\frac{\partial \ell_i}{\partial \beta} = w_i \sum_{j=1}^{J_i} \text{grad\_vec}[j] \cdot X_{ij}^T = w_i \, X_i^T \, \text{grad\_vec}
$$

The full gradient is accumulated as a single BLAS matrix-vector product, identically to MNL.

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

### 3.3 Gradient with Respect to $\delta$

Since $\frac{\partial V_{ij}}{\partial \delta_a} = \mathbf{1}_{j = a}$, the gradient entries are the corresponding elements of `grad_vec`, scattered to the appropriate positions in $\theta$:

$$
\frac{\partial \ell_i}{\partial \delta_a} = w_i \cdot \text{grad\_vec}[a]
$$

The same free-ASC convention as MNL applies (first inside alternative's ASC excluded when no outside option).

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

### 3.4 Gradient with Respect to $\lambda_k$

Define the within-nest probability-weighted mean utility:

$$
\bar{V}_k = \sum_{j \in B_k} P(j \mid k) \cdot V_{ij}
$$

**For the chosen nest ($k = k_i$).** The log-probability decomposes as:

$$
\log P_{ij_i} = \underbrace{\frac{V_{ij_i}}{\lambda_{k_i}} - \log I_{k_i}}_{\log P(j_i \mid k_i)} + \underbrace{\lambda_{k_i} \log I_{k_i} - \log D_i}_{\log P_{k_i}}
$$

Using $\frac{\partial \log I_k}{\partial \lambda_k} = -\bar{V}_k / \lambda_k^2$:

$$
\frac{\partial \log P(j_i \mid k_i)}{\partial \lambda_{k_i}} = \frac{\bar{V}_{k_i} - V_{ij_i}}{\lambda_{k_i}^2}
$$

$$
\frac{\partial \log P_{k_i}}{\partial \lambda_{k_i}} = (1 - P_{k_i})\!\left(\log I_{k_i} - \frac{\bar{V}_{k_i}}{\lambda_{k_i}}\right)
$$

Combining:

$$
\frac{\partial \ell_i}{\partial \lambda_{k_i}} = w_i \left[(1 - P_{k_i})\!\left(\log I_{k_i} - \frac{\bar{V}_{k_i}}{\lambda_{k_i}}\right) + \frac{\bar{V}_{k_i} - V_{ij_i}}{\lambda_{k_i}^2}\right]
$$

**For a non-chosen nest ($k \neq k_i$).** The conditional probability $P(j_i \mid k_i)$ is independent of $\lambda_k$, so only the nest probability contributes:

$$
\frac{\partial \log P_{k_i}}{\partial \lambda_k} = -P_k \!\left(\log I_k - \frac{\bar{V}_k}{\lambda_k}\right)
$$

$$
\frac{\partial \ell_i}{\partial \lambda_k} = -w_i \, P_k \!\left(\log I_k - \frac{\bar{V}_k}{\lambda_k}\right)
$$

The common factor $\log I_k - \bar{V}_k / \lambda_k$ is labeled `term_in_brackets` in the code.

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

---

## 4. Hessian Computation

**This section documents the Hessian of the *negated* log-likelihood.** The function `nl_loglik_hessian_parallel` returns $H(\theta) = -\nabla^2 \ell(\theta)$, the same quantity that `invert_hessian()` expects (positive semi-definite at the MLE) and inverts equilibrated (§5.8). The sign convention matches the numeric oracle `nl_loglik_numeric_hessian` (which differences the negated gradient), so both functions are interchangeable as inputs to `invert_hessian()`.

Two implementations are available:

- `nl_loglik_hessian_parallel` — **default** (`se_method = "hessian"`): single-pass analytical Hessian derived below. Validated against the numeric oracle at a maximum absolute difference of $\approx 2.6 \times 10^{-8}$ across the package's test fixtures, well below the $10^{-6}$ tolerance those tests enforce. At extreme $\lambda_k < 0.1$, the oracle's own finite-difference accuracy degrades; the analytical Hessian remains finite and symmetric throughout.
- `nl_loglik_numeric_hessian` — retained oracle (`se_method = "numeric"`): central finite differences on the analytical gradient with step $\epsilon_i = 10^{-6} \cdot \max(|\theta_i|, 1)$. Use for diagnostic comparison or whenever a direct verification of the analytical path is required.

---

### 4.1 Notation and Scope

All notation follows §§0–3. Subscripts $i$ (individual), $j/a/b$ (alternative local indices within $i$'s choice set, 0-based), and $k$/$l$ (nest indices, 0-based) are used throughout. Additional symbols specific to this section:

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| $k_i$ | 0-based index of the chosen nest ($-1$ when outside option is chosen) |
| $c_a$ | 0-based local index of the chosen inside alternative |
| $\bar{V}_k$ | $\sum_{j \in B_k} P(j \mid k) \cdot V_{ij}$ — $P(\cdot \mid k)$-weighted mean utility in nest $k$ |
| $T_k$ | $\log I_k - \bar{V}_k / \lambda_k$ — the "bracket term" from §3.4 |
| $\widetilde{V}^2_k$ | $\sum_{j \in B_k} P(j \mid k) \cdot V_{ij}^2$ — conditional second moment |
| $\mathrm{VarV}_k$ | $\widetilde{V}^2_k - \bar{V}_k^2$ — $P(\cdot\mid k)$-weighted variance of $V$ in nest $k$ |
| $\mathbf{m}_k$ | $\sum_{j \in B_k} P_{ij} \cdot \mathbf{x}_{ij}$ — $P_{ij}$-weighted mean of $X$ in nest $k$ ($K$-vector) |
| $\mathbf{c}_k$ | $\sum_{j \in B_k} P(j \mid k) \cdot \mathbf{x}_{ij}$ — $P(\cdot\mid k)$-weighted mean of $X$ in nest $k$ ($K$-vector) |
| $\mathbf{S}^{(2)}_k$ | $\sum_{j \in B_k} P_{ij} \cdot \mathbf{x}_{ij} \mathbf{x}_{ij}^T$ — $P_{ij}$-weighted second moment of $X$ ($K \times K$) |
| $\mathbf{Q}_k$ | $\sum_{j \in B_k} P(j \mid k) \cdot \mathbf{x}_{ij} \mathbf{x}_{ij}^T$ — $P(\cdot\mid k)$-weighted second moment of $X$ ($K \times K$) |
| $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_i$ | $\sum_j P_{ij} \cdot \mathbf{x}_{ij}$ — $P_{ij}$-weighted global mean of $X$ for individual $i$ ($K$-vector) |

The negated per-individual log-likelihood contribution is $f_i = -w_i \log P_{i,c_a}$. The full Hessian is the sum $H = \sum_{i=1}^N H^{(i)}$ where $H^{(i)} = -w_i \nabla^2 \log P_{i,c_a}$.

---

### 4.2 V-Space Hessian $Q_i$

Because $V_{ij} = \mathbf{x}_{ij} \beta + \delta_j$ is linear in $\beta$ and $\delta$, the second derivatives with respect to these parameters factor through the $m_i \times m_i$ V-space Hessian. Define:

$$
Q_i[a, b] = -\frac{\partial^2 \log P_{i,c_a}}{\partial V_{ia} \, \partial V_{ib}}
$$

Starting from the gradient formula (§3.1):

$$
g[a] = \frac{\partial \log P_{i,c_a}}{\partial V_{ia}}
= -P_{ia} + \left(1 - \frac{1}{\lambda_{k_i}}\right) \mathbf{1}_{a \in B_{k_i}} P(a \mid k_i) + \frac{\mathbf{1}_{a = c_a}}{\lambda_{k_i}}
$$

differentiating with respect to $V_{ib}$ yields:

$$
\frac{\partial g[a]}{\partial V_{ib}} = -\frac{\partial P_{ia}}{\partial V_{ib}} + \left(1 - \frac{1}{\lambda_{k_i}}\right) \mathbf{1}_{a \in B_{k_i}} \frac{\partial P(a \mid k_i)}{\partial V_{ib}}
$$

**Partial derivative of $P_{ia}$ with respect to $V_{ib}$.** Write $k_a = k(a)$, $k_b = k(b)$. Expanding $P_{ia} = P(a \mid k_a) \cdot P_{k_a}$ via the product rule and using $\partial P_{k_a}/\partial V_{ib} = P_{k_a}[\mathbf{1}_{k_b=k_a} P(b\mid k_a) - P_{ib}]$:

$$
\frac{\partial P_{ia}}{\partial V_{ib}}
= P_{ia} \left\{
  \mathbf{1}_{k_a = k_b}\left[
    \frac{\mathbf{1}_{a=b}}{\lambda_{k_a}}
    + P(b \mid k_a)\left(1-\frac{1}{\lambda_{k_a}}\right)
  \right]
  - P_{ib}
\right\}
$$

**Partial derivative of $P(a \mid k_i)$ with respect to $V_{ib}$.** Non-zero only when $a \in B_{k_i}$:

$$
\frac{\partial P(a \mid k_i)}{\partial V_{ib}}
= \frac{1}{\lambda_{k_i}} \mathbf{1}_{k_b = k_i} P(b \mid k_i) \left(\mathbf{1}_{a=b} - P(a \mid k_i)\right)
$$

**Combined V-space Hessian (correct formula).** Negating and combining:

$$
\boxed{
Q_i[a, b]
= P_{ia} \left\{
  \mathbf{1}_{k_a = k_b}\left[
    \frac{\mathbf{1}_{a=b}}{\lambda_{k_a}}
    +P(b \mid k_a)\left(1-\frac{1}{\lambda_{k_a}}\right)
  \right]
  - P_{ib}
\right\}
- \underbrace{\mathbf{1}_{k_a = k_i} \mathbf{1}_{k_b = k_i} \cdot \frac{1 - 1/\lambda_{k_i}}{\lambda_{k_i}} \cdot P(a \mid k_i)\bigl(\mathbf{1}_{a=b} - P(b \mid k_i)\bigr)}_{C_{a,b}: \text{ chosen-nest correction}}
}
$$

The chosen-nest correction $C_{a,b}$ is nonzero only when both $a$ and $b$ are in the chosen nest $k_i$ (and $k_i \geq 0$). It arises from the $(1 - 1/\lambda_{k_i})$ factor in $g[a]$ coupling the conditional probability gradient back to $V_{ib}$.

**Structural notes and MNL limit:**

- For $k_a \neq k_b$: $Q_i[a,b] = -P_{ia} P_{ib}$ (cross-nest entries are the
  *negative* product of marginal probabilities, the familiar multinomial covariance term).
- **MNL limit** ($\lambda_k = 1$ for all $k$): $Q_i[a,b] = P_{ia}(\mathbf{1}_{a=b} - P_{ib})$, the standard multinomial Hessian of $-\log P_{c_a}$. Own diagonal $= P_{ia}(1-P_{ia})$; off-diagonal $= -P_{ia}P_{ib}$. The chosen-nest correction vanishes because $1 - 1/\lambda_{k_i} = 0$.
- When the outside option is chosen ($k_i = -1$) or when $\lambda_{k_i} = 1$ (singleton chosen nest), $C_{a,b} = 0$ for all pairs.

*Implementation note:* The implementation never forms $Q_i$ as an $m_i \times m_i$ matrix: it forms one column at a time, for each row with a free constant (§4.4, §4.8), and the outer-product decomposition used for the beta-beta block (§4.3) needs no entry of it.

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

---

### 4.3 Beta-Beta Block

Since $\partial V_{ij}/\partial \beta_r = x_{ij,r}$:

$$
H^{(i)}_{\beta_r, \beta_s} = w_i \sum_{a} \sum_{b} x_{ia,r} \cdot Q_i[a,b] \cdot x_{ib,s}
= w_i \, \mathbf{X}_i^T \mathbf{Q}_i \mathbf{X}_i
$$

The matrix product is decomposed into three terms that can be accumulated in a single nest-level pass, exploiting the outer-product structure of $Q_i$:

**Term A — universal outer product (subtracted):**
$$
-w_i \, \bar{\mathbf{x}}_i \, \bar{\mathbf{x}}_i^T
$$

This arises from the $-P_{ia} P_{ib}$ term universal to all pairs: $\sum_{a,b} x_{ia,r} P_{ia} P_{ib} x_{ib,s} = \bar{x}_{i,r} \bar{x}_{i,s}$.

**Term B — per-nest within-nest correction (added), summed over all nests $k$:**
$$
+w_i \sum_{k} \left[ \left(1 - \frac{1}{\lambda_k}\right) \mathbf{m}_k \mathbf{c}_k^T + \frac{1}{\lambda_k} \mathbf{S}^{(2)}_k \right]
$$

For singleton nests ($\lambda_k = 1$): $(1 - 1/\lambda_k) = 0$, so the contribution reduces to $\mathbf{S}^{(2)}_k$.

**Term C — chosen-nest correction (subtracted), only when $k_i \geq 0$:**
$$
-w_i \cdot \frac{1 - 1/\lambda_{k_i}}{\lambda_{k_i}} \left( \mathbf{Q}_{k_i} - \mathbf{c}_{k_i} \mathbf{c}_{k_i}^T \right)
$$

Here $\mathbf{Q}_{k_i} - \mathbf{c}_{k_i}\mathbf{c}_{k_i}^T$ is the $P(\cdot\mid k_i)$-weighted covariance of $X$ within the chosen nest.

**Full beta-beta block (Hessian of the negated log-likelihood; positive semi-definite at the MLE):**
$$
H^{(i)}_{\beta\beta}
= w_i \left[
  -\bar{\mathbf{x}}_i \bar{\mathbf{x}}_i^T
  + \sum_k \!\left(\!\left(1-\frac{1}{\lambda_k}\right)\mathbf{m}_k \mathbf{c}_k^T + \frac{1}{\lambda_k}\mathbf{S}^{(2)}_k\right)
  - \mathbf{1}_{k_i \geq 0} \cdot \frac{1-1/\lambda_{k_i}}{\lambda_{k_i}} \!\left(\mathbf{Q}_{k_i} - \mathbf{c}_{k_i}\mathbf{c}_{k_i}^T\right)
\right]
$$

**MNL limit check.** At $\lambda_k = 1$ for all $k$: Term B $= \sum_k \mathbf{S}^{(2)}_k = \mathbf{X}_i^T \mathrm{diag}(P_i) \mathbf{X}_i$; Term C vanishes; the formula yields the standard MNL expression $w_i(\mathbf{X}_i^T \mathrm{diag}(P_i) \mathbf{X}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}}_i \bar{\mathbf{x}}_i^T)$.

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

---

### 4.4 Beta-Delta and Delta-Delta Blocks

Since $\partial V_{ij}/\partial \delta_a = \mathbf{1}_{j=a}$, these blocks are direct projections of $Q_i$ onto free-ASC alternatives.

**Delta-delta block** (for free-ASC alternatives $a'$ and $b'$):
$$
H^{(i)}_{\delta_{a'}, \delta_{b'}} = w_i \cdot Q_i[a', b']
$$

**Beta-delta block** (for covariate index $r$ and free-ASC alternative $b'$):
$$
H^{(i)}_{\beta_r, \delta_{b'}} = w_i \sum_{a} x_{ia,r} \cdot Q_i[a, b']
= w_i \, \bigl(\mathbf{X}_i^T \mathbf{Q}_i[:, b']\bigr)_r
$$

Both blocks use the column $Q_i[:, b']$ of each row $b'$ with a free constant, formed once (§4.8). No additional auxiliary quantities are required.

**ASC normalization.** Without an outside option, the first inside alternative's ASC is fixed to zero: free-ASC alternatives satisfy `alt_idx0[a] > 0`, mapped to theta positions `delta_start_idx + alt_idx0[a] - 1`.

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

---

### 4.5 Lambda-V Cross Derivative

The lambda parameters enter nonlinearly through both $\log I_k$ and the nest probabilities, so cross-derivatives between $\lambda_k$ and $\beta/\delta$ must be computed via the chain rule. Define:

$$
d^{(k)}_b = \frac{\partial g_{\lambda_k}}{\partial V_{ib}}, \qquad
g_{\lambda_k} = \frac{\partial \log P_{i,c_a}}{\partial \lambda_k}
$$

Key intermediates (derived from §3.4):

$$
\frac{\partial T_k}{\partial V_{ib}} = -\mathbf{1}_{k(b)=k} P(b \mid k) \frac{V_{ib} - \bar{V}_k}{\lambda_k^2}, \qquad
\frac{\partial P_k}{\partial V_{ib}} = P_k \bigl[\mathbf{1}_{k(b)=k} P(b \mid k) - P_{ib}\bigr]
$$

**For non-chosen nests ($k \neq k_i$), using $g_{\lambda_k} = -P_k T_k$:**
$$
d^{(k)}_b = P_k T_k P_{ib}
+ \mathbf{1}_{k(b)=k} P_k P(b \mid k) \left[\frac{V_{ib} - \bar{V}_k}{\lambda_k^2} - T_k\right]
$$

The first term is a universal "shift" proportional to $P_{ib}$; the second is the within-nest correction active only for $b \in B_k$.

**For the chosen nest ($k = k_i$, only when $k_i \geq 0$), using $g_{\lambda_{k_i}} = (1-P_{k_i})T_{k_i} + (\bar{V}_{k_i} - V_{c_a})/\lambda_{k_i}^2$:**
$$
d^{(k_i)}_b = P_{k_i} T_{k_i} P_{ib}
- \frac{\mathbf{1}_{b = c_a}}{\lambda_{k_i}^2}
+ \mathbf{1}_{k(b)=k_i} P(b \mid k_i) \left[
  -P_{k_i} T_{k_i}
  + \frac{V_{ib} - \bar{V}_{k_i}}{\lambda_{k_i}^2} \left(P_{k_i} - 1 + \frac{1}{\lambda_{k_i}}\right)
  + \frac{1}{\lambda_{k_i}^2}
\right]
$$

The extra $-1/\lambda_{k_i}^2$ term for $b = c_a$ arises from differentiating the $(\bar{V}_{k_i} - V_{c_a})/\lambda_{k_i}^2$ component of the chosen-nest gradient.

---

### 4.6 Lambda-Beta and Lambda-Delta Blocks

Using $\partial V_{ib}/\partial \beta_r = x_{ib,r}$ and $\partial V_{ib}/\partial \delta_{b'} = \mathbf{1}_{b=b'}$:

$$
H^{(i)}_{\lambda_k, \beta_r} = -w_i \sum_{b} d^{(k)}_b \cdot x_{ib,r}
= -w_i \, \bigl(\mathbf{X}_i^T \mathbf{d}^{(k)}\bigr)_r
$$

$$
H^{(i)}_{\lambda_k, \delta_{b'}} = -w_i \, d^{(k)}_{b'}
$$

Both are filled symmetrically. Singleton nests (theta index $= -1$) contribute no rows or columns to these blocks.

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

---

### 4.7 Lambda-Lambda Block

Differentiating $g_{\lambda_k}$ with respect to $\lambda_l$, using:
$$
\frac{\partial T_k}{\partial \lambda_k} = \frac{\mathrm{VarV}_k}{\lambda_k^3} \geq 0, \qquad
\frac{\partial P_k}{\partial \lambda_k} = P_k (1 - P_k) T_k, \qquad
\frac{\partial P_k}{\partial \lambda_l} = -P_k P_l T_l \;(l \neq k), \qquad
\frac{\partial T_k}{\partial \lambda_l} = 0 \;(l \neq k)
$$

**Off-diagonal $k \neq l$ (any combination of chosen/non-chosen nests):**
$$
H^{(i)}_{\lambda_k, \lambda_l} = -w_i \, P_k P_l T_k T_l
$$

This formula holds uniformly regardless of whether $k$ or $l$ equals $k_i$. It can be negative (whenever $T_k$ and $T_l$ share the same sign), reflecting correlation between nest-level inclusive values.

**Diagonal $k \neq k_i$ (non-chosen nest):**
$$
H^{(i)}_{\lambda_k, \lambda_k} = w_i \left[ P_k (1 - P_k) T_k^2 + \frac{P_k \, \mathrm{VarV}_k}{\lambda_k^3} \right]
$$

The first term is a Fisher-information-type squared-gradient term; the second is positive and captures curvature from $T_k$'s dependence on $\lambda_k$ through the within-nest utility variance.

**Diagonal $k = k_i$ (chosen nest, only when $k_i \geq 0$):**
$$
H^{(i)}_{\lambda_{k_i}, \lambda_{k_i}} = w_i \left[
  P_{k_i}(1 - P_{k_i}) T_{k_i}^2
  - \frac{(1 - P_{k_i}) \mathrm{VarV}_{k_i}}{\lambda_{k_i}^3}
  + \frac{\mathrm{VarV}_{k_i}}{\lambda_{k_i}^4}
  + \frac{2(\bar{V}_{k_i} - V_{c_a})}{\lambda_{k_i}^3}
\right]
$$

The chosen-nest diagonal differs from the non-chosen formula because the $(\bar{V}_{k_i} - V_{c_a})/\lambda_{k_i}^2$ term in $g_{\lambda_{k_i}}$ contributes $-\mathrm{VarV}_{k_i}/\lambda_{k_i}^4 - 2(\bar{V}_{k_i} - V_{c_a})/\lambda_{k_i}^3$ when differentiated. Since the chosen alternative tends to have above-average utility within its nest ($V_{c_a} \geq \bar{V}_{k_i}$ in expectation), the last term is typically negative, making the chosen-nest diagonal somewhat smaller than the non-chosen counterpart.

When the outside option is chosen ($k_i = -1$), all lambda diagonals use the non-chosen formula.

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

---

### 4.8 Single-Pass Implementation and Auxiliary Accumulations

All six blocks are accumulated in a **single parallel pass** over individuals. The per-nest auxiliary quantities below are accumulated in an inner loop over alternatives at $O(m_i)$ cost before any block is computed, for the nests the situation offers only: a nest it does not offer has zero sums and contributes nothing.

**Per-nest scalars** (zero-initialized per individual, indexed by nest $k$):

| Quantity | Formula | Blocks that use it |
|----------|---------|-------------------|
| $\bar{V}_k$ | $\sum_{j \in B_k} P(j\mid k) V_j$ | $T_k$, lambda-lambda, lambda-V cross |
| $\widetilde{V}^2_k$ | $\sum_{j \in B_k} P(j\mid k) V_j^2$ | $\mathrm{VarV}_k$ for lambda-lambda diagonal |
| $T_k$ | $\log I_k - \bar{V}_k/\lambda_k$ | lambda-lambda (all entries), lambda-V cross |
| $\mathrm{VarV}_k$ | $\widetilde{V}^2_k - \bar{V}_k^2$ | lambda-lambda diagonal |

**Per-nest K-vectors:**

| Quantity | Formula | Blocks that use it |
|----------|---------|-------------------|
| $\mathbf{m}_k$ | $\sum_{j \in B_k} P_{ij} \mathbf{x}_j$ | beta-beta Term B |
| $\mathbf{c}_k$ | $\sum_{j \in B_k} P(j\mid k) \mathbf{x}_j$ | beta-beta Terms B and C |

**Per-nest $K \times K$ matrices:**

| Quantity | Formula | Blocks that use it |
|----------|---------|-------------------|
| $\mathbf{S}^{(2)}_k$ | $\sum_{j \in B_k} P_{ij} \mathbf{x}_j \mathbf{x}_j^T$ | beta-beta Term B |
| $\mathbf{Q}_k$ | $\sum_{j \in B_k} P(j\mid k) \mathbf{x}_j \mathbf{x}_j^T$ | beta-beta Term C (formed for the chosen nest $k_i$ only) |

**Global per-individual:** $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_i = \sum_j P_{ij} \mathbf{x}_j = \sum_k \mathbf{m}_k$ (beta-beta Term A).

**Compact blocks.** A situation's terms touch only its *compact block*: the $K$
coefficients, the dissimilarities of the non-singleton nests it offers (those whose
$\log I_k$ is finite), and the free constants of its alternatives, in increasing order.
$Q_i$ is formed a column at a time (no $m_i \times m_i$ matrix), the symmetric
$K \times K$ sums are kept as packed upper triangles, and the lambda-lambda block runs over
the pairs of touched nests. A situation's blocks thus cost $O(m_i^2K + m_iK^2)$, whatever
the number of alternatives in the model; its probabilities still visit every nest.

**OpenMP structure.** The outer loop over individuals is parallelized with dynamic
scheduling. Each thread adds into its own packed upper triangle while the threads'
triangles fit in a budget (2 GiB by default), and above it into a shared result: each
thread keeps the coefficients' rows private (and the dissimilarities', while the threads'
copies of them fit in the budget) and adds the rest atomically. All of it is allocated
before the loop, once the kernel's memory estimate has been checked against
`options(choicer.max_memory)` or the physical memory.

**Symmetrization and sanitization.** $Q_i$ and Term B's $\mathbf{m}_k\mathbf{c}_k^T$ are
symmetric in exact arithmetic ($P_{ij} = P_k P(j\mid k)$, so
$\mathbf{m}_k = P_k\mathbf{c}_k$) but not in floating point. Each entry therefore
receives the mean of its two transposed terms, $H \leftarrow (H + H^T)/2$ computed term
by term (halving is exact except for subnormal terms, so no running sum is doubled on the
way); any remaining non-finite entries are zeroed.

**Singleton-nest handling.** Singleton nests ($\lambda_k = 1$, theta index $= -1$) contribute nothing to the lambda-lambda, lambda-beta, or lambda-delta blocks. Their beta-beta contribution via Term B simplifies to $\mathbf{S}^{(2)}_k$ (since $1 - 1/\lambda_k = 0$).

**Per-individual weights.** Every contribution is multiplied by $w_i$ (WESML weight; equals 1 for unweighted data).

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

---

## 5. Implementation Details

### 5.1 Parameter Vector Structure

The full parameter vector $\theta$ is organized as:

| Block | Indices | Length | Description |
|-------|---------|--------|-------------|
| $\beta$ | $[0, K)$ | $K$ | Coefficients for design matrix $X$ |
| $\lambda$ | $[K, K + K_\lambda)$ | $K_\lambda$ | Non-singleton nest dissimilarity parameters |
| $\delta$ | $[K + K_\lambda, K + K_\lambda + J_{\text{asc}})$ | $0$, $J-1$, or $J$ | Free alternative-specific constants |

where $K_\lambda$ is the number of non-singleton nests and $J_{\text{asc}}=0$ when
`use_asc = FALSE`, $J-1$ without an outside option, or $J$ with an outside option.

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

### 5.2 Singleton Nest Handling

At startup, the implementation identifies which nests are singletons (contain exactly one alternative). These nests:
- Have their $\lambda$ fixed to 1 (no contribution to the upper-level logit denominator beyond their single utility term).
- Are excluded from the estimated parameter vector.
- Are tracked via `nest_k_to_theta_idx`, an integer vector of length $K$ where entry $k$ holds the corresponding index in $\theta$ for non-singleton nests and $-1$ for singletons.

This ensures that the NL model degenerates gracefully to MNL on a per-nest basis when nests are singletons.

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

### 5.3 Data Organization

- **Design matrix $X$**: Stacked matrix of dimension $(\sum_i M_i) \times K$, where $M_i$ is the number of inside alternatives for individual $i$.
- **`alt_idx`**: 1-based indices mapping rows of $X$ to global alternative IDs.
- **`nest_idx`**: 1-based nest assignment of length $J$ (number of unique inside alternatives), not length $\sum M_i$. Accessed via `nest_idx.elem(alt_idx0_i)` to handle varying choice sets.
- **`choice_idx`**: 1-based local row position of the chosen inside alternative within
  each situation's block; 0 for the outside option.
- **Prefix sums $S$**: Used for efficient slicing into the stacked data: $S_i = \sum_{j < i} M_j$.

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

### 5.4 Base Utility Pre-computation

Prior to the parallel loop, all systematic utilities $V_{ij} = X_{ij}\beta + \delta_j$ are computed in a single pass:

```
base_util = X * beta                 // single BLAS dgemm
if use_asc: base_util += delta[alt_idx0]
```

This avoids redundant matrix-vector products inside the per-individual loop.

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

### 5.5 OpenMP Parallelization

The implementation parallelizes over individuals using OpenMP:
- Each thread keeps local accumulators (the log-likelihood and gradient, or a packed upper
  triangle of the Hessian or BHHH matrix, §4.8; one thread adds into the result itself) and
  its working arrays (the probabilities, the individual's nests, a copy of its covariate
  rows where Armadillo's product needs one), all allocated before the parallel loop once the
  kernel's memory estimate has been checked, so that no individual allocates.
- The Hessian's and BHHH matrix's triangles are added after the loop in thread order (above
  the budget, the shared entries atomically during it); the log-likelihood and gradient in
  an order that can vary between calls.
- The loops over the dissimilarities (their gradient, scores and Hessian terms) run over
  the nests the individual faces, and so do the inclusive values and nest probabilities
  where every $\lambda_k$ is positive and the nests outnumber the alternatives on average
  (§2.7).
- Dynamic scheduling balances load across individuals with varying choice set sizes, each
  dispatch handing a thread about 256 stacked rows, at least one individual
  (`CHOICER_CHUNK_ROWS` at compile time), and fewer where the largest choice set has more
  than eight times the mean rows, so that no dispatch holds more than about 2,048.
- The elasticity and diversion-ratio kernels add each individual's terms into a
  $J \times J$ sum, as the multinomial logit's do: one thread into the result itself, $T$
  threads into copies of their own while those fit in 2 GiB, and beyond that into the
  shared result atomically, the outside option's row and column kept per thread; its memory
  is checked before it is allocated.

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

### 5.6 Negated Objectives

The likelihood/gradient kernel returns:
- $-\ell(\theta)$ (negated log-likelihood)
- $-\nabla\ell(\theta)$ (negated gradient)

for compatibility with minimization routines (e.g., `nloptr`) that minimize a loss function rather than maximize a likelihood.
The analytical and numeric Hessian kernels return $-\nabla^2\ell$; the BHHH kernel
instead returns the positive-semidefinite OPG information approximation
$\sum_iw_is_is_i^T$.

### 5.7 Finite-Value Guards

The likelihood kernel replaces a non-finite chosen log probability by $-10^{10}$.
If the final negated objective is non-finite it returns $10^{10}$ and a zero gradient;
isolated non-finite gradient entries are zeroed. The analytical Hessian skips a situation
whose chosen log probability is non-finite, adds the mean of each pair of transposed terms
(§4.8), and replaces any remaining non-finite entries by zero. These rules are optimizer failure guards, not part
of the regular finite-parameter nested-logit criterion; encountering them calls for
rescaling or revising the specification. The likelihood kernel's list also holds
`overflow`, `TRUE` where it replaced anything (a clamped log probability, the sentinel,
a gradient entry set to zero, as where an unchosen nest's inclusive value overflows and
the nest drops out of the denominator, leaving the chosen probability finite and too
high): the optimizers do not see it, and the polish (§5.9) rejects a trial point that
sets it.

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp); the flag, `logit_sanitize()` in [src/choicer_internal.h](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/choicer_internal.h)*

### 5.8 Inverting the Information

Every reported variance of $\hat\theta$ is the inverse of an estimate of the information
matrix, or a sandwich built on one: $V = \mathcal{I}^{-1}$ with $\mathcal{I}$ the negated
Hessian $-\nabla^2 \ell(\hat\theta)$ of §4 (`se_method = "hessian"`, or its
finite-difference oracle under `"numeric"`) or the BHHH matrix
$\sum_i w_i\, s_i s_i^{\top}$ of §5.6 (`"bhhh"`), or $V = A^{-1} B A^{-1}$ with the bread
$A$ and meat $B$ of §7.3 (`"sandwich"`) or §7.5 (`"cluster"`). In the data's units the
diagonal of $\mathcal{I}$ can span many orders of magnitude: a covariate measured in
thousands next to one measured in thousandths, or the constant of an alternative a handful
of individuals chose next to that of one most chose. Inverted as it is, such a matrix can
be refused as computationally singular although only the units make it so (`solve()`
refuses a matrix whose estimated reciprocal condition number falls below the machine
epsilon, and the units alone can push it there), and a sandwich built on it can lose
digits. Every fit, whatever the coordinates its optimizer used (`scale_vars`, `"none"` by
default here; §1.5 of the [mixed logit article](mixed_logit_math.html)), therefore inverts
the equilibrated matrix:

$$
V = D\,(D \mathcal{I} D)^{-1} D, \qquad
D = \mathrm{diag}(d), \quad d = 2^{\,\mathrm{round}(-\frac{1}{2}\log_2 |\mathrm{diag}(\mathcal{I})|)},
$$

with $\mathrm{diag}(\mathcal{I})$ the vector of the diagonal entries of $\mathcal{I}$ and
the functions applied elementwise: $d$ holds the powers of two nearest, on a log scale, to
the inverse square roots of the diagonal's magnitudes, with an entry of 1 where the
diagonal entry is zero or not finite and every entry clamped to $[2^{-500}, 2^{500}]$. For
the sandwich, $V = D\,V_D\,D$ with $V_D = (DAD)^{-1} (DBD) (DAD)^{-1}$ and $D$ from $A$.
Any $D$ leaves $V$ unchanged in exact arithmetic, and powers of two make the products with
$D$ exact too, barring overflow or underflow: only the $LU$ factorization and the solves
round (for the sandwich, also the symmetrization below), on a matrix whose diagonal is
within a factor of two of one in magnitude except where a diagonal entry is zero or not
finite, or an entry of $d$ is clamped. The magnitude of the diagonal is used so that an
information that is not positive definite (away from a maximum) is equilibrated too, and
its negative variances reported: their standard errors are `NA`, with a message.

$D \mathcal{I} D$ is formed in one working copy, which LAPACK factors in place ($LU$ with
partial pivoting) with `solve()`'s checks: a pivot that is exactly zero is an error, and
so, when every factor is finite, is a reciprocal condition number (estimated in the
1-norm) below the machine epsilon; either error leaves the fit without a variance, its
standard errors `NA`, with a message. The identity is then solved against the factors into
the result, as reference LAPACK's `dgesv` does for `solve()`, with two $p \times p$
matrices besides $\mathcal{I}$ ($p$ the number of parameters) where `solve()` holds three.
The sandwich is solved twice against the factors of $DAD$, first $(DAD)\,Y = DBD$ and then
the transposed system $(DAD)^{\top} V_D^{\top} = Y^{\top}$, without forming an inverse:
two $p \times p$ matrices besides $A$ and $B$ where an explicit inverse and two products
hold four, and $4\tfrac{2}{3} p^3$ operations against $6\tfrac{2}{3} p^3$. $V_D$ is
symmetrized, $(V_D + V_D^{\top})/2$, before $D$ is applied. At $p = 17{,}000$ each such
matrix takes 2.3 GB. The working copy is freed as the call returns, and the package's own
passes over whole matrices (the scaling, the scan of the factors for non-finite entries,
the transposition and the symmetrization) run in parallel over columns, without sums
across threads, so they do not depend on the number of threads. The fit and post-hoc
`vcov(fit, type = )` and `wesml_vcov()` take this same route.

Against an exact computation on the package's reference battery and tests (963 inversions
of 477 distinct matrices, of 2 to 13 parameters), a raw inversion refused 52 as singular;
equilibrated, 44 of them, with raw condition numbers from $4.5 \times 10^{18}$ to
$1.2 \times 10^{28}$, had condition numbers below 20 and came out with standard errors
within about $10^{-15}$ relative of exact, while the other eight stayed ill-conditioned or
singular. Equilibration removes the ill-conditioning that the parameters' units cause, not
the likelihood's own: a matrix that stays ill-conditioned after it (a likelihood nearly
flat along a combination of parameters, which no rescaling of the parameters one by one
removes) keeps only the digits its condition number allows, by any inversion, and one
singular to working precision is refused either way. Some of the package's nested logit
test designs give such matrices, with condition numbers up to $7 \times 10^{12}$ after
equilibration; two more, near $10^{16}$, are refused (six inversions). Where an exact
variance is zero, as at some degenerate test fits, the computed one is rounding noise of
either sign, and a negative one gets an `NA` standard error like any negative variance.

*Code reference: `invert_hessian()`, `.sandwich_combine()` and `.jacobi_scale()` in [R/classes.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/classes.R); `equilibrated_inverse()` and `equilibrated_sandwich()` in [src/vcov.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/vcov.cpp).*

### 5.9 Polishing the Optimizer's Solution

`run_nestlogit(polish = )` follows the optimizer with the Newton phase of the
[mixed logit](mixed_logit_math.html) (§5.7 there), which finishes the climb to the maximum
the optimizer approached and certifies it; the estimator does not change. With $g$ the
gradient of $-\ell$ and $C$ the curvature, the analytic information
$\mathcal{I} = -\nabla^2 \ell$ of §4 (`polish = "newton"`) or the BHHH matrix
$\sum_i w_i\, s_i s_i^{\top}$ of §5.6 (`"bhhh"`, its weights unsquared), the polish
converges when the Newton decrement $\nu = \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^{\top} C^{-1} g$, over the
mean weight, falls below `tol_decrement` ($10^{-8}$). On a positive definite $\mathcal{I}$
the remaining Newton step then moves every linear combination of the estimates by at most
$\sqrt{2\nu}$ of its Hessian standard error; with `"bhhh"` the bound is in robust standard
errors (for an unweighted fit; with weights, in the metric of $\mathcal{I}^{-1}
\mathcal{B} \mathcal{I}^{-1}$ with $\mathcal{B}$'s weights unsquared), and a small BHHH
decrement on its own shows only a stationary point. The steps,
their damping and maximum length, the line search and the projection onto the
dissimilarities' bound are those of the mixed logit's §5.7.

**Curvature.** For given dissimilarities all at most 1 the log-likelihood is concave in
$(\beta, \delta)$: each $\log P_{ij} = V_{ij}/\lambda_k + (\lambda_k - 1) \log I_k - \log
\sum_l \exp(\lambda_l \log I_l)$ (the sum also holding the outside option's 1, where there
is one) adds to a linear term a nonpositive multiple of a log-sum-exp, which is convex in
the utilities, and subtracts a log-sum-exp, convex and nondecreasing in each argument, of
the convex functions $\lambda_l \log I_l$. It need not be concave jointly with $\lambda$,
nor in $(\beta, \delta)$ where some $\lambda_k > 1$: the information can be indefinite away
from the maximum, where the steps are damped (Levenberg–Marquardt), and a maximum the
polish certifies can be local. The dissimilarities keep their lower bound of $10^{-16}$.
Where the steps drive one to that bound, they are damped at nearly every iteration and the
polish does not report convergence. In one of the package's test designs (200 choice
situations) a fit from a poor start went there, 24 log-likelihood units below the interior
maximum that a polish from another stop certified in six steps; in two others every start
ended at the bound. Refit from other starts: where they all end there, the likelihood's
supremum is at the bound, the dissimilarity has no interior estimate and no polish
certifies the fit, and the nest is to be revised.

**What is held.** The constants of inside alternatives without a finite estimate are held
at the optimizer's values, and the certificate concerns the other parameters given them,
with one exception. An alternative chosen wherever it is offered has a positive score for
its constant at every $\theta$, and is held, as in the multinomial logit. A never-chosen
alternative $j$ in nest $k$ is held only where $k$ is a singleton or $\lambda_k \le 1$ at
the optimizer's solution. Where $j$ is offered and the alternative chosen, $j_i$, belongs
to another nest, its constant's score is $-P_{ij} < 0$; where $j_i$ is a nest-mate, it is

$$
\frac{\partial \log P_{ij_i}}{\partial \delta_j} = P(j \mid k) \left(1 - \frac{1}{\lambda_k} - P_k\right),
$$

negative for $\lambda_k \le 1$ but positive for $\lambda_k > 1$ where the nest's
probability $P_k$ is below $1 - 1/\lambda_k$. Above 1 the constant can then have a finite
estimate, which the polish seeks, so it is moved. Both terms vanish in proportion to
$P(j \mid k)$ as $\delta_j \to -\infty$: where they are negative on balance there, the
constant still has no finite estimate, and the polish moves it down until its share of the
decrement is below the tolerance. It may then certify a point where the constant, and its
standard error, are set by `tol_decrement`: in `mode_choice` with a never-chosen copy of
bus (its generalized cost raised by 5), whose public nest has $\lambda \approx 1.95$, about
$-47$, its standard error about $2 \times 10^4$. A polish that held such a constant at
$\lambda_k \le 1$ and ends with $\lambda_k > 1$ does not report convergence, nor does one
that moved it and ends with $\lambda_k \le 1$, where it has no finite estimate. The
reference's divergence is treated as in the
[multinomial logit](multinomial_logit_math.html) (§12.7 there): the held constants must
anchor every other constant that can rise (a never-chosen one cannot rise without bound,
since wherever it is offered the chosen alternative lies outside any set of never-chosen
ones). A never-chosen base
alternative, the reference, is treated as a moved constant (the others move against it),
so that rule applies only where its nest is a singleton or ends with $\lambda_k \le 1$.

**Other limits.** A nest that no situation offers two of has a dissimilarity on which the
likelihood does not depend. Its score, its BHHH column and its Hessian entries are zero in
exact arithmetic. The score and the BHHH column are exactly zero at the default start of
0.5, where the optimizer then leaves it (1/λ is exact there), and of rounding size
elsewhere; the Hessian's diagonal holds a rounding residue everywhere, 0.5 included (of
either sign, about $10^{-16}$ to $6 \times 10^{-14}$ in a test design). The BHHH polish
leaves such a dissimilarity out of its steps, as without information or as stalled, and
does not report convergence. Where the Hessian's residue is positive, the Newton polish
certifies the other parameters, leaving the dissimilarity at 0.5 or moving it on the
score's rounding elsewhere; where it is negative, the steps are damped and the polish does
not certify. Its standard error is huge (about $10^{7}$ in a test design) or `NA`. A trial point fails where the likelihood kernel reports
that its objective or gradient is not the log-likelihood's (§5.7 above): a log probability
clamped to $-10^{10}$, a total that is not finite, or a gradient entry set to zero, as
where an unchosen nest's inclusive value overflows and the nest drops out of the
denominator, which leaves the chosen probability finite and too high. The optimizers do not
see that report.

**Scales and the variance.** The maximum step and the stall rule are measured in the
optimizer's coordinates $m$ (§1.5 of the mixed logit article). Under the nested logit's
default `scale_vars = "none"` those would be the parameters' own units, so the scales come
instead from the BHHH diagonal at the optimizer's solution projected onto the bound, as
`"bhhh"` takes them at the start values: one pass of the gradient kernel. With half of the
covariates rescaled by $10^3$ and the other half by $10^{-3}$, 20 steps at unit scales left
a decrement of 1,054 to 1,786, where 8 or 9 at these scales certified the maximum. The
variance is computed at the polished estimates, by `se_method`, and the polish's last
curvature, evaluated at the point it returns, is not evaluated again where it is the
variance's own matrix: after `"newton"`, the analytic Hessian of `"hessian"` and the bread
of `"sandwich"` and `"cluster"`; after `"bhhh"`, the BHHH matrix of `"bhhh"`.
`se_method = "numeric"` takes its own numerical Hessian.

**On census- and claims-style designs** (2,504 and 2,602 alternatives in 50 nests, with
24,560 and 245,031 choice situations; 499 and 500 alternatives with 17,339 and 153,721;
ten covariates; constants without a finite estimate removed; single runs at eleven
threads, times modeled from the kernels' calls), the default fit reached its limit of
1,000 evaluations on three of the four designs: 0.35 and 15.8 log-likelihood units short of
the maximum on the census-style ones (up to 6.7 standard errors), $8 \times 10^{-5}$ on the
smaller claims-style one; the larger stopped by its tolerance, $2 \times 10^{-7}$ short.
The Newton polish certified the maximum in 3 and 5 steps on the census-style designs, for
about a tenth of the fit's time, and in one step on the claims-style ones. Stopping the
optimizer after 100 evaluations and polishing took about a fifth of the time of the default
fit and its polish, and `scale_vars = "bhhh"` stopped at the maximum in 50 to 66
evaluations on three of the four designs.

*Code reference: `run_polish()`, `.polish_held()`, `.polish_anchors()`, `.polish_fit()`
and `.polish_scales()` in [R/classes.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/classes.R);
`newton_step()` in [src/newton.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/newton.cpp);
the curvature, the hold rule (`.nl_nest_lambda()`) and the reuse in `run_nestlogit()`,
[R/nestlogit_utils.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/nestlogit_utils.R);
the kernels' report, `logit_sanitize()` in
[src/choicer_internal.h](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/choicer_internal.h).*

## 6. Post-Estimation Quantities

### 6.1 Choice Probabilities (predict)

The joint probability is the decomposition from §2.1:

$$
P_{ij} = P(j \mid k(j)) \cdot P_{k(j)}
$$

with $P(j \mid k)$ and $P_k$ given in §§2.3–2.4. `nl_predict` returns individual-level probabilities $P_{ij}$ and systematic utilities $V_{ij}$ for every observation row. `nl_predict_shares` aggregates over individuals to obtain weighted market shares:

$$
\hat{s}_j = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \, P_{ij}}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i}
$$

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

---

### 6.2 Elasticities

#### 6.2.1 Semi-elasticity with respect to utility

Let $r = k(j)$ be the nest of the responding alternative $j$ and $s = k(a)$ be the nest of the perturbed alternative $a$. From §3.1, the derivative of $\log P_{ij}$ with respect to the systematic utility of any alternative $a$ is:

$$
\frac{\partial \log P_{ij}}{\partial V_{ia}}
= \frac{\mathbf{1}_{a=j}}{\lambda_r}
+ \left(1 - \frac{1}{\lambda_r}\right)\mathbf{1}_{s=r} \, P(a \mid r)
- P_{ia}
$$

This is the general expression; the gradient formula in §3.1 applies it only to the *chosen* alternative, whereas here we evaluate it for all pairs $(j, a)$ to construct the full elasticity matrix.

#### 6.2.2 Elasticity of $P_{ij}$ with respect to covariate $k$ of alternative $a$

Since $\partial V_{ia} / \partial x_{ia,k} = \beta_k$:

$$
E_{ij,ia}^{k}
= \frac{\partial P_{ij}}{\partial x_{ia,k}} \cdot \frac{x_{ia,k}}{P_{ij}}
= \beta_k \, x_{ia,k} \cdot \frac{\partial \log P_{ij}}{\partial V_{ia}}
$$

Substituting the three cases:

| Case | Condition | Semi-elasticity $\partial \log P_{ij}/\partial V_{ia}$ |
|------|-----------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| Own | $a = j$ | $\dfrac{1}{\lambda_r} + \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\lambda_r}\right) P(j \mid r) - P_{ij}$ |
| Cross, same nest | $s = r,\; a \neq j$ | $\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\lambda_r}\right) P(a \mid r) - P_{ia}$ |
| Cross, different nest | $s \neq r$ | $-P_{ia}$ |

**Reduction to MNL.** When $\lambda_k = 1$ for all nests the within-nest term $(1 - 1/\lambda_r)$ vanishes and the conditional probability drops out, giving $\partial \log P_{ij}/\partial V_{ia} = \mathbf{1}_{a=j} - P_{ia}$, which is exactly the MNL semi-elasticity (§3.1 of the MNL document).

**Outside option.** When an outside option is present it occupies its own singleton nest with $\lambda_0 = 1$ and $x_{i0,k} = 0$. Its row (responding = outside option) has semi-elasticity $-P_{ia}$ for every inside alternative $a$ (different nest, §3.1); its column (perturbed = outside option) is identically zero because $\beta_k \cdot 0 = 0$.

The implementation accumulates $w_i \cdot E_{ij,ia}^k$ across individuals and divides by
$\sum_i w_i$ to produce a weighted average of *individual probability elasticities*.
This is not generally the elasticity of an aggregate share under a common market-level
perturbation when attributes vary across situations. Rows index responding alternatives
and columns perturbed alternatives.

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

---

### 6.3 Diversion Ratios

#### 6.3.1 Definition

The utility-based diversion ratio from losing alternative $j$ to receiving alternative
$k$ is:

$$
DR(j \to k) = -\frac{\partial Q_k / \partial V_{ij}}{\partial Q_j / \partial V_{ij}}
$$

where $Q_m = \sum_i w_i P_{im}$ is aggregate demand and the perturbation is through the systematic utility of the *losing* alternative $j$.

#### 6.3.2 Partial derivatives of demand

Using $\partial P_{im}/\partial V_{ij} = P_{im} \cdot (\partial \log P_{im}/\partial V_{ij})$ and the semi-elasticity from §6.2.1, the three cases with $r = k(j)$:

$$
\frac{\partial P_{im}}{\partial V_{ij}} =
\begin{cases}
P_{ij}\!\left[\dfrac{1}{\lambda_r} + \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\lambda_r}\right) P(j \mid r) - P_{ij}\right] & m = j \\[6pt]
P_{im}\!\left[\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\lambda_r}\right) P(j \mid r) - P_{ij}\right] & k(m) = r,\; m \neq j \\[6pt]
-P_{im} \, P_{ij} & k(m) \neq r
\end{cases}
$$

#### 6.3.3 Utility Perturbation and Covariate Interpretation

The implemented matrix is defined with respect to a common additive perturbation of
$V_{ij}$. If a fixed-coefficient attribute of alternative $j$ receives the same additive
change $dx$ in every situation, $dV_{ij}=\beta_r dx$, so the common scalar cancels:

$$
DR(j \to k)
= -\frac{\beta_r dx\sum_i w_i \,(\partial P_{ik}/\partial V_{ij})}
         {\beta_r dx\sum_i w_i \,(\partial P_{ij}/\partial V_{ij})}
= -\frac{\sum_i w_i \,(\partial P_{ik}/\partial V_{ij})}
         {\sum_i w_i \,(\partial P_{ij}/\partial V_{ij})}
$$

It is in this additive-shift sense that NL diversion is independent of the chosen fixed
covariate. For a proportional perturbation $dx_i=x_{ij,r}d\log x$, the values
$x_{ij,r}$ remain inside both population sums and generally do **not** cancel. The kernel
does not compute that attribute-specific proportional diversion. In MXL even a common
additive perturbation of a random-coefficient attribute carries draw-specific
$\beta_{ir}^s$, so the coefficient cannot be factored out.

#### 6.3.4 Population aggregation and column-sum property

Define:

$$
\text{num}(k, j) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \left(-\frac{\partial P_{ik}}{\partial V_{ij}}\right), \qquad
\text{den}(j) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \frac{\partial P_{ij}}{\partial V_{ij}}
$$

so that $DR(j \to k) = \text{num}(k,j) \,/\, \text{den}(j)$ for $k \neq j$.

**Columns sum to 1.** The fundamental identity $\sum_{m} \partial P_{im}/\partial V_{ij} = 0$ (probabilities sum to 1 for every individual and every perturbation direction, including the outside option when present) gives:

$$
\sum_{k \neq j} \frac{\partial P_{ik}}{\partial V_{ij}} = -\frac{\partial P_{ij}}{\partial V_{ij}}
\implies
\sum_{k \neq j} \text{num}(k, j) = \text{den}(j)
\implies
\sum_{k \neq j} DR(j \to k) = 1
$$

When an outside option is present it acts as both a source (it can lose demand) and a destination (it can receive diverted demand), so it appears in both the row index $k$ and the column index $j$ of the $J_{\text{total}} \times J_{\text{total}}$ diversion matrix, and the column sums still equal 1 over all alternatives including the outside option.
Because its systematic utility is fixed at zero in estimation, the outside-as-source
column is a derivative with respect to a hypothetical perturbation of that normalized
utility, not an available outside-option covariate.

#### 6.3.5 Reduction to MNL at $\lambda = 1$

When all $\lambda_k = 1$ the cross-same-nest case collapses to the cross-different-nest case ($\partial P_{im}/\partial V_{ij} = -P_{im} P_{ij}$ for $m \neq j$) and the own case gives $\partial P_{ij}/\partial V_{ij} = P_{ij}(1 - P_{ij})$. Substituting:

$$
DR(j \to k)\big|_{\lambda=1}
= \frac{\sum_i w_i \, P_{ij} \, P_{ik}}{\sum_i w_i \, P_{ij} (1 - P_{ij})}
$$

which is the MNL diversion ratio (§6.3 of the MNL document).

*Code reference: [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp)*

---

### 6.4 BLP Share Inversion

#### 6.4.1 Problem statement

Given observed market shares $s_j^*$, find the ASC vector $\delta$ such that the NL model reproduces those shares, with $\beta$ and $\lambda$ held at their values:

$$
\hat{s}_j(\delta) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \, P_{ij}(\delta)}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i} = s_j^* \quad \forall j
$$

where $P_{ij}(\delta) = P(j \mid k(j)) \cdot P_{k(j)}$. The identification of $\delta$, the
checks of the targets, the stopping rule and the result are the multinomial logit's (§7 of
the [multinomial logit article](multinomial_logit_math.html)); this section gives the
nested logit's step.

#### 6.4.2 The step

With $r = \log s^* - \log \hat{s}(\delta)$, $b$ the outside option (or, without one, the
reference of $j$'s component) and $\rho_j = r_j - r_b$, the step is the multinomial
logit's (§7.3 of the [multinomial logit article](multinomial_logit_math.html)): a common
shift $\tau$ of the component's free constants, then the exact diagonal of the
derivative of $\rho$ on the rest,

$$
\delta_j \leftarrow \delta_j + \kappa \left(\tau + \frac{\rho_j - h_j \tau}{D_j}\right),
\qquad
D_j = \frac{A_{jj}}{\hat{s}_j} + \frac{C_{jb}}{\hat{s}_b},
\qquad
h_j = \frac{C_{jb}}{\hat{s}_j} + \sum_k \frac{C_{kb}}{\hat{s}_b},
$$

for alternative $j$ in nest $g$, where $\kappa \in (0, 1]$ is `damping` (default 1),
$\tau$ solves $\sum_j \hat{s}_j (\rho_j - h_j \tau) = 0$,

$$
A_{jj} = \frac{\partial \hat{s}_j}{\partial \delta_j}
= \frac{\sum_i w_i P_{ij}\left(\frac{1 - P_i(j \mid g)}{\lambda_g} + P_i(j \mid g) - P_{ij}\right)}{\sum_i w_i},
$$

and $C_{jb} = -\partial \hat{s}_b / \partial \delta_j$: $\sum_i w_i P_{ij} P_{i0}$ over $\sum_i
w_i$ with an outside option, and without one

$$
C_{jb} = \frac{\sum_i w_i P_{ib}\left(\frac{1 - \lambda_g}{\lambda_g} P_i(j \mid g)\, 1\{b \in g\} + P_{ij}\right)}{\sum_i w_i}.
$$

The nested logit's share Jacobian is symmetric (its shares are the gradient of the
log-sum, for any $\lambda_g > 0$) and its rows sum to zero, so $-h_j$ is the exact rate
at which $\rho_j$ responds to the common shift, as in the logit. Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes's (1995)
contraction, `method = "original"`, takes $\kappa r_j$ ($\kappa (r_j - r_b)$ without an
outside option, the reference held): no shift, no outside-share correction, and 1 in place
of $D_j$. It therefore overshoots within a nest: its step's derivative there is about
$1/\lambda_g$, and its iteration can diverge where $\lambda_g$ is small (it failed on 8
of the 18 simulated designs we tried with $\lambda_g \le 0.4$, and on none with larger
$\lambda_g$) unless damped by about $\lambda_g$. The exact diagonal
carries the $1/\lambda_g$, so no damping is needed. For a nest's dominant alternative,
$1 - P_i(j \mid g)$ is formed as the sum of its nest-mates' conditional probabilities,
since $\lambda_g$ can be as small as $10^{-16}$, where the difference loses every digit.
The logit's other safeguards apply: the step's cap, its halving where the shares are not
finite, and the restarts.

#### 6.4.3 Nests with $\lambda_g > 1$

Where $\lambda_g > 1$ nest-mates are complements: raising $\delta_j$ raises the nest's
inclusive value, and with it the shares of $j$'s nest-mates where the nest is small. Two
safeguards apply.

- An alternative whose co-choice with the base is negative ($b$ in its nest, without an
  outside option) has a diagonal $D_j$ of at least 1: its exact diagonal nets out the
  complementarity and can be near zero or negative.
- The diagonal $D_j$ is at least $(1 + \lambda_g)/(2\lambda_g)$ times the one the same
  probabilities give with $\lambda_g = 1$ ($\sum_i w_i P_{ij}(1 - P_{ij})/\sum_i w_i$ over
  $\hat{s}_j$, plus $\sum_i w_i P_{ij}P_{ib}/\sum_i w_i$ over $\hat{s}_b$). A common shift
  of a nest's constants moves its shares as in a logit, with derivative about 1, while a
  shift within the nest moves them with derivative about $1/\lambda_g$; the exact diagonal
  is close to the latter, so its step would overshoot the common shift by up to
  $\lambda_g$ and diverge for $\lambda_g$ above 2. The factor relaxes the two directions
  equally: the step's error then contracts by about $(\lambda_g - 1)/(\lambda_g + 1)$ in
  each.

On 80 simulated designs with $\lambda$ from 1.05 to 5, nests of 2 and 5 alternatives, 12
and 60 alternatives and heterogeneous choice sets, solved to $10^{-12}$, the step
converged on every one, in a median 0.32 of Berry's evaluations and never more (with an
outside option, Berry's contraction needed 129 to 170 evaluations, the step 9 to 70).

#### 6.4.4 The layout of `delta`

Without an outside option, `delta` is a full length-$J$ vector, normalized by subtracting
its first entry, so the returned baseline is zero. With an outside option, supplied and
returned `delta` contain the $J$ inside ASCs only, and `target_shares` has $J+1$ entries,
the outside option's first.

**Note on the `lambda` argument.** `nl_blp_contraction` expects a *full* length-$n_{\text{nests}}$ vector where singleton nests have their entry set to 1, every entry positive and finite. This differs from the estimated parameter block $\lambda$ in $\theta$, which contains only non-singleton entries. The caller is responsible for expanding the estimated lambdas into the full vector before invoking the inversion.

*Code reference: `NlBlpModel` and `nl_blp_solve()` in [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp), over [src/blp_engine.h](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/blp_engine.h).*

### 6.5 Willingness to Pay

Utility is linear in covariates, so willingness to pay is the same marginal rate of substitution as in the MNL model: for attribute $k$ and price coefficient $\alpha = \beta_p$,

$$
\mathrm{WTP}_k = -\frac{\beta_k}{\alpha},
\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}} = \sqrt{\nabla g^T \, \hat{V}_{(k,p)} \, \nabla g},
\quad
\nabla g = \begin{pmatrix} -1/\alpha \\ \beta_k/\alpha^2 \end{pmatrix}
$$

with $\hat{V}_{(k,p)}$ the $2 \times 2$ block of the coefficient covariance. The nest parameters $\lambda$ rescale within-nest substitution but do not enter the ratio of marginal utilities, so they affect WTP only through the estimated covariance of $(\beta_k, \alpha)$. ASCs may also be used as the numerator ($-\delta_j/\alpha$). See §8 of the MNL document for the full derivation and caveats.

*Code reference: [R/wtp.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/wtp.R)*

### 6.6 Consumer Surplus and the Nested Logsum

For the nested logit, expected maximum utility is the two-level logsum below plus the
scenario-invariant extreme-value location constant (omitted by `logsum()`, as in MNL):

$$
\mathrm{logsum}_i = \log D_i = \log\left( \sum_{l} \exp\big(\lambda_l \log I_l\big) \; [+\, 1] \right),
\qquad
\log I_l = \log \sum_{j \in B_l \cap C_i} \exp\!\left(\frac{V_{ij}}{\lambda_l}\right)
$$

where the $+1 = \exp(0)$ term appears when an outside option is present and singleton nests have $\lambda_l = 1$ (§5.2). Both levels are computed with the max-subtraction trick (§2.7).

Two useful identities:

- **Reduction to MNL.** With all $\lambda_l = 1$, $\lambda_l \log I_l = \log \sum_{j \in B_l} \exp(V_{ij})$ and the nested logsum collapses to the MNL logsum $\log \sum_j \exp(V_{ij})$.
- **Outside-option link.** Since $P_{i0} = 1 / D_i$ (§2.5), the logsum equals $-\log P_{i0}$ — a direct consistency check against the probability kernel.

Expected consumer surplus follows Train (2009, Ch. 3) exactly as in the MNL case:

$$
\mathbb{E}[CS_i] = \frac{\mathrm{logsum}_i}{-\alpha}
$$

with the same caveats: no income effects, and CS levels inherit the ASC normalization, so only differences across scenarios (counterfactual `newdata` vs. baseline) are meaningful. The implementation reports point estimates for NL (the delta-method SE of the mean CS is currently provided for MNL only; Krinsky–Robb resampling of the coefficients is the practical interval method here).
The routine does not enforce $\alpha<0$; interpreting $-\alpha$ as positive marginal
utility of income requires the analyst to verify the estimated sign.

*Code reference: [R/surplus.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/surplus.R)*

### 6.7 Goodness of Fit

The measures are model-agnostic and identical to §10 of the MNL document, computed from the NL log-likelihood and predicted probabilities:

- **McFadden pseudo R²**: $R^2 = 1 - \ell(\hat\theta)/\ell_0$ and $R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - (\ell(\hat\theta) - K)/\ell_0$, with $K$ counting all estimated parameters including the $\lambda$ block.
- **Equal-shares null** (default, exact for unbalanced sets and weights): $\ell_0 = -\sum_i w_i \log(M_i + \mathbf{1}_{\text{outside}})$.
- **Market-shares null** (constants-only closed form):
  $\ell_0 = c\sum_j N_j \log(s_j)$, where $c$ is the common weight; requires
  identical choice-set composition across individuals and uniform weights. The
  constants-only model is itself an MNL—at $\beta = 0$ and free ASCs the nest structure
  is not identified from constant shares—so the same closed form applies.
- **Hit rate**: weighted share of choice situations whose observed choice has the highest predicted NL probability; with an outside option the outside good competes with $P_{i0} = 1 - \sum_j P_{ij}$.

*Code reference: [R/gof.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/gof.R)*

---

## 7. Choice-Based Sampling and WESML Weighting

### 7.1 Endogenous Stratified (Choice-Based) Sampling

Under *random* (exogenous) sampling each choice situation is drawn independently of its
outcome. Under **choice-based** (endogenous stratified) sampling the strata are defined by
the **chosen alternative** $j_i$ and situations are drawn with stratum-specific
frequencies — for example, deliberately oversampling individuals who chose a rare
alternative. Let $Q(j)$ be the population share of alternative $j$ and $H(j)$ the sample
share of choosers of $j$.

Unlike the MNL special case (a full set of ASCs leaves the slopes consistent), the **nested
logit has no such free pass**: the dissimilarity parameters $\lambda_l$ enter the within-
and between-nest probabilities nonlinearly, so choice-based sampling generally biases the
slopes $\beta$, the constants $\delta$, **and** the $\lambda$ block. Weighting is therefore
required for consistent estimation of the population parameters.

### 7.2 The WESML Weighted Log-Likelihood

Manski and Lerman (1977) restore consistency by weighting each situation's contribution by
the ratio of population to sample share of its chosen alternative,

$$
w_i = \frac{Q(j_i)}{H(j_i)},
\qquad
\ell^{W}(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \log P_{i j_i}(\theta).
$$

The maximizer $\hat\theta$ is invariant to multiplying every $w_i$ by a common positive
constant, so the weights may be normalized to mean 1 without changing the estimates.

### 7.3 Robust (Sandwich) Variance: the $w^2$ Meat

WESML is a weighted M-estimator solving $\sum_i w_i\, s_i(\hat\theta) = 0$, where
$s_i = \partial \log P_{i j_i}/\partial\theta$ is the **full per-situation score over the
$\beta$, $\lambda$ and $\delta$ blocks** ($\S$3) and $H_i$ its Hessian ($\S$4). Its robust
(Huber–White) asymptotic variance is the **sandwich**

$$
V = A^{-1} B A^{-1}, \qquad
A = \sum_{i} w_i\,(-H_i), \qquad
B = \sum_{i} w_i^{2}\, s_i s_i^{\top}.
$$

The weight enters the **bread** $A$ linearly, but the **meat** $B$ carries the weight
**squared**: the contribution of situation $i$ to the estimating equation is $w_i s_i$, so
its variance involves $(w_i s_i)(w_i s_i)^{\top} = w_i^{2}\, s_i s_i^{\top}$. The score
$s_i$ is assembled exactly as in the gradient kernel ($\S$3.3–3.4): the $\beta$ and $\delta$
blocks from `grad_vec`, and the $\lambda_l$ blocks from the per-nest expression
$(\,\mathbf{1}\{l = l_i\} - P_{il}\,)\big[\log I_{il} - \lambda_l^{-1}\!\sum_{j\in B_l}
P_{ij|l} V_{ij}\big] + \mathbf{1}\{l=l_i\}\,\lambda_l^{-2}\big(\sum_{j\in B_l} P_{ij|l}V_{ij}
- V_{ij_i}\big)$, with singleton nests ($\lambda_l \equiv 1$) contributing no score.

As in the MNL/MXL cases, both naive variances are wrong under weighting: the inverse-Hessian
$A^{-1}$ assumes the information-matrix equality $A = B$ (which fails once the $w_i$ are
non-degenerate), and ordinary BHHH/OPG $\big(\sum_i w_i\, s_i s_i^{\top}\big)^{-1}$ uses the
weight to the first power, not the second. The sandwich is invariant to the weight scale:
$A \to cA$, $B \to c^2 B$, hence $V \to A^{-1} B A^{-1}$.

### 7.4 Scope: Robust vs. Design-Based Variance

The estimator implemented here is the **robust weighted-M-estimator (Huber–White)
variance**, with uncentered meat $B = \sum_i w_i^{2}\, s_i s_i^{\top}$ — the asymptotic
variance under **variable-probability sampling**. The smaller stratum-centered
(design-based) variance for a **fixed-quota** design is out of scope; see Manski & McFadden
(1981) and Cosslett (1981).

### 7.5 Implementation and Cluster-Robust Extension

The meats come from compiled kernels that never form the $N\times p$ matrix of
weight-free scores (singleton lambdas are not parameters, so the meats have no rows for
them): the BHHH
kernel `nl_bhhh_parallel()` adds $w_i\,s_is_i^T$ over each situation's compact block
(§4.8), with `weights = w` for the BHHH information and `weights = w^2` for the robust
meat, so that

$$
A=\texttt{nl\_loglik\_hessian\_parallel}(\widehat\theta;w),
\qquad B=\texttt{nl\_bhhh\_parallel}(\widehat\theta;w^2)=\sum_i w_i^2 s_is_i^T.
$$

For a fit whose selected method is the numeric NL Hessian, the bread uses the numeric
oracle instead. The fit-time variance (`se_method`), `vcov(fit, type = )`, the
recomputation of a variance dropped from a fit and `wesml_vcov()` all compute it from the
same kernels (`.assemble_score_vcov()`, or `compute_hessian()` for a Hessian or BHHH variance
recomputed lazily), so a fit's variance is the one `vcov()` returns post hoc: bit for bit at
one thread, and up to the last bits with more. For cluster labels $g(i)$,
`se_method = "cluster"` uses

$$
B_{\mathrm{cluster}}=\sum_g
\left(\sum_{i:g(i)=g}w_is_i\right)
\left(\sum_{i:g(i)=g}w_is_i\right)^T,
$$

formed by `nl_cluster_meat_parallel()` without the score matrix either (the situations
sorted by cluster, each cluster's weighted compact scores summed over the parameters its
situations touch), with no finite-cluster correction. These matrices are combined as
$V=A^{-1}BA^{-1}$, computed equilibrated by two solves against the $LU$ factors of the
equilibrated bread, without forming an inverse (§5.8). User-facing entry points: `wesml_weights()`
computes the Manski--Lerman weights from the population shares $Q$, while
`sample_by_choice()` draws a choice-based sample and attaches those weights;
`run_nestlogit(..., se_method = "sandwich")`
estimates with the robust variance; `wesml_vcov()` returns it post hoc. Passing
`run_nestlogit(..., weights_col = )` collapses a row-level weight column to one weight per
choice situation (validated constant within `id`), and a provenance guard prevents a
WESML-labeled sample from being silently fit unweighted.

*Code reference: `nl_bhhh_parallel()` / `nl_cluster_meat_parallel()` in [src/nestlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/nestlogit.cpp); `.assemble_score_vcov()`, `.logit_meat()` and `.sandwich_combine()` in [R/classes.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/classes.R) (`.score_meat()` there forms the same meats from the score matrix of `nl_scores_parallel()`, as the tests' reference); `equilibrated_sandwich()` in [src/vcov.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/vcov.cpp); `wesml_weights()` / `sample_by_choice()` in [R/sampling.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/sampling.R).*
